Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•We introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for con-
structing and validating apparently credible but factually
misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks, yield-
ing 5,933 quality-controlled instances from the DeepRe-
search Bench.
•We evaluate six open-source framework–LLM configu-
rations and one closed-source system, showing that even
limited exposure to misleading knowledge can lead to
false-conclusion adoption.
•We characterize how adoption varies with source prop-
erties, exposure conditions, lifecycle stage, framework
choice,andbackbonechoice,andshowthatpre-andpost-
research defenses reduce but do not eliminate it.

positive_signals: The paper introduces MisKnow-Agent, a controlled framework for constructing and validating apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances from DeepResearch Bench.
The paper evaluates six open-source framework-LLM configurations and one closed-source system, showing that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can lead to false-conclusion adoption.

The paper characterizes how adoption varies with source properties, exposure conditions, lifecycle stage, framework choice, and backbone choice, and shows that pre- and post-research defenses reduce but do not eliminate it.

The paper positions its work against prior studies that examine short-horizon responses to misleading context or explicitly adversarial settings, rather than ambient reliability risks in open-web research.

The paper states that prior Deep Research evaluations assess report quality, citation correctness, retrieval faithfulness, and claim-level factuality but do not systematically isolate how misleading knowledge propagates within the workflow.
The paper reports that search-result rank has limited influence, with mean FCAR of 66.2%, 65.5%, and 64.5% under front, spread, and back placement conditions.
